# Markov Chain Monte Carlo(MCMC)

## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler: the problem]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 65%;"}


So far, we have covered conjugate and semi-conjugate posteriors — these gave us nice closed forms. But what if the joint posterior looks something like this?

. . .


$$p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto \left(\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} e^{-\frac{(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{\sigma^{2(\alpha+1)}} e^{-\beta/\sigma^2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\tau} e^{-\frac{(\mu-m)^2}{2\tau^2}} \cdot \frac{\lambda^{a-1} e^{-b\lambda}}{1 + e^{-\gamma(\mu - \lambda\bar{x})}}$$

. . .

**Direct sampling is hard** — the joint posterior can live in high dimensions with no tractable form.

. . .

**Key insight:** even though the joint $p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x})$ is hard to sample from directly, if we can derive each parameter's *full conditional* distribution — conditioning on all other parameters — those are often much simpler:

$$p(\theta_j \mid \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{j-1}, \theta_{j+1}, \ldots, \theta_p, \mathbf{x}) \quad \text{for each } j = 1, \ldots, p$$

. . .

These full conditionals are just slices of the joint — and slices of a nasty joint are often recognizable distributions we know how to sample from.

. . .

[So instead of tackling the full joint at once, we sample one parameter at a time —  treating all others as fixed constants. Each step is a simple **univariate** draw.]{style="color: red;"}
:::


## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler: the idea]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}

Start with some initial guess $(\theta_1^{(1)}, \theta_2^{(1)})$. Then for $t = 2, 3, \ldots$:

. . .

**Step 1.** Sample $\theta_1^{(t)}$ from $p(\theta_1 \mid \theta_2^{(t-1)}, \mathbf{x})$
— treat $\theta_2$ as **fixed**, sample $\theta_1$

. . .

**Step 2.** Sample $\theta_2^{(t)}$ from $p(\theta_2 \mid \theta_1^{(t)}, \mathbf{x})$
— treat the **new** $\theta_1$ as fixed, sample $\theta_2$

. . .

Each draw is a **1D problem** — much easier than the full 2D joint.

:::

## [Gibbs sampler: a familiar example]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 68%;"}

[Let's refer to the bivariate normal example from Dr. Li's Lecture 6 slides.]{style="color: red;"}

. . . 

To build intuition, consider a target we actually know:

$$\begin{pmatrix}\theta_1\\\theta_2\end{pmatrix} \sim N_2\left(\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},\ \begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho\\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}\right)$$

. . .

Even though we could sample this directly, suppose we only use the full conditionals:

$$\theta_1 \mid \theta_2 \sim N(\rho\theta_2,\ 1-\rho^2), \qquad \theta_2 \mid \theta_1 \sim N(\rho\theta_1,\ 1-\rho^2)$$

. . .

**Why this example?** This is not a posterior — it is a 
plain bivariate normal whose exact shape we already know. 
Running Gibbs here lets us verify the algorithm works, 
before applying it to our actual posterior where 
no exact answer exists.
:::



## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler: why it works]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 68%;"}

The sequence
$$(\theta_1^{(1)}, \theta_2^{(1)}),\ (\theta_1^{(2)}, \theta_2^{(2)}),\ \ldots$$
forms a **Markov chain** — each draw depends only on the previous one.

. . .

Under mild conditions, this chain **converges** to the joint posterior as its stationary distribution:

$$(\theta_1^{(t)}, \theta_2^{(t)}) \xrightarrow{t \to \infty} p(\theta_1, \theta_2 \mid \mathbf{x})$$

. . .

This means after enough iterations, our draws are (approximately) samples from the posterior we actually want — even though we never sampled from it directly.

. . .

> **Burn-in:** the early part of the chain (before convergence) is discarded.

:::

## [Gibbs Sampler — Interactive Animation]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}

```{=html}
<div id="gibbs-root">
<div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:center;gap:10px;margin-bottom:6px;font-size:12px;">
  <button id="gb-step">Step</button>
  <button id="gb-play">▶ Play</button>
  <button id="gb-reset">Reset</button>
  <label>Speed
    <input type="range" id="gb-spd" min="100" max="2000" value="800" step="100">
    <span id="gb-spdv">800ms</span>
  </label>
  <label>ρ
    <input type="range" id="gb-rho" min="-0.95" max="0.95" value="0.95" step="0.05">
    <span id="gb-rhov">0.95</span>
  </label>
  <label>σ²
    <input type="range" id="gb-var" min="0.2" max="3" value="1" step="0.1">
    <span id="gb-varv">1.0</span>
  </label>
  <span id="gb-lbl" style="opacity:0.6;">Step: 0 / 100</span>
</div>

<div id="gb-ann" style="min-height:28px;font-size:12px;padding:4px 8px;margin-bottom:4px;
  border-left:3px solid #2a72c8;background:rgba(42,114,200,0.07);border-radius:3px;
  color:#1a1a1a;line-height:1.4;"></div>

<canvas id="gb-cv" width="900" height="420"
  style="width:100%;border:1px solid #ccc;border-radius:6px;"></canvas>
</div>

<script>
setTimeout(function(){
  var root = document.getElementById('gibbs-root');
  if(!root) return;
  var cv   = root.querySelector('#gb-cv');
  var ctx  = cv.getContext('2d');
  var ann  = root.querySelector('#gb-ann');
  var W=900,H=420,pad=55,plotW=W-pad*2,plotH=H-pad*2;
  var xl=[-8,8],yl=[-8,8];
  var N=100;
  var chain=[],cur=0,playing=false,timer=null;

  function getParams(){
    return {
      rho:  parseFloat(root.querySelector('#gb-rho').value),
      sig2: parseFloat(root.querySelector('#gb-var').value)
    };
  }

  function randn(){
    var u,v;
    do{u=Math.random();}while(!u);
    do{v=Math.random();}while(!v);
    return Math.sqrt(-2*Math.log(u))*Math.cos(2*Math.PI*v);
  }

  function buildChain(rho,sig2){
    var sig=Math.sqrt(sig2);
    var c=[[6*sig,-6*sig]];
    for(var i=1;i<=N;i++){
      var p=c[c.length-1];
      var z1=rho*p[1]+Math.sqrt(sig2*(1-rho*rho))*randn();
      c.push([z1,p[1]]);
      var z2=rho*z1+Math.sqrt(sig2*(1-rho*rho))*randn();
      c.push([z1,z2]);
    }
    return c;
  }

  function px(x,y){
    return [
      pad+(x-xl[0])/(xl[1]-xl[0])*plotW,
      pad+(1-(y-yl[0])/(yl[1]-yl[0]))*plotH
    ];
  }

  function bgauss(x,y,rho,sig2){
    var z=(x*x-2*rho*x*y+y*y)/(sig2*(1-rho*rho));
    return Math.exp(-z/2);
  }

  function drawContours(rho,sig2){
    var levels=[0.05,0.15,0.35,0.55,0.75,0.90];
    var cols=['#e8e6fb','#ccc9f5','#b3afee','#9a95e7','#837de2','#6a63db'];
    var gN=80;
    var xs=Array.from({length:gN},function(_,i){return xl[0]+(xl[1]-xl[0])*i/(gN-1);});
    var ys=Array.from({length:gN},function(_,j){return yl[0]+(yl[1]-yl[0])*j/(gN-1);});
    var vals=xs.map(function(x){return ys.map(function(y){return bgauss(x,y,rho,sig2);});});
    var dx=plotW/(gN-1),dy=plotH/(gN-1);
    for(var li=levels.length-1;li>=0;li--){
      var lv=levels[li];
      ctx.beginPath();
      for(var i=0;i<gN-1;i++){
        for(var j=0;j<gN-1;j++){
          var v=[vals[i][j],vals[i+1][j],vals[i+1][j+1],vals[i][j+1]];
          var cnt=v.filter(function(vv){return vv>=lv;}).length;
          if(cnt>0&&cnt<4){
            var pt=px(xs[i]+(xs[1]-xs[0])/2,ys[j]+(ys[1]-ys[0])/2);
            ctx.rect(pt[0]-dx/2,pt[1]-dy/2,dx,dy);
          }
        }
      }
      ctx.fillStyle=cols[li]; ctx.fill();
    }
  }

  function drawAxes(){
    ctx.strokeStyle='rgba(0,0,0,0.1)'; ctx.lineWidth=0.5;
    ctx.fillStyle='rgba(0,0,0,0.4)';   ctx.font='11px sans-serif';
    for(var v=-6;v<=6;v+=2){
      var pt1=px(v,0),pt2=px(0,v);
      ctx.beginPath();ctx.moveTo(pt1[0],pad);ctx.lineTo(pt1[0],H-pad);ctx.stroke();
      ctx.beginPath();ctx.moveTo(pad,pt2[1]);ctx.lineTo(W-pad,pt2[1]);ctx.stroke();
      ctx.textAlign='center'; ctx.fillText(v,pt1[0],H-pad+14);
      ctx.textAlign='right';  ctx.fillText(v,pad-6,pt2[1]+4);
    }
    ctx.fillStyle='rgba(0,0,0,0.65)'; ctx.font='13px sans-serif';
    ctx.textAlign='center'; ctx.fillText('\u03b8\u2081',W/2,H-8);
    ctx.save();ctx.translate(14,H/2);ctx.rotate(-Math.PI/2);
    ctx.fillText('\u03b8\u2082',0,0);ctx.restore();
  }

  function drawGuide(upTo){
    if(upTo<=0||upTo>=chain.length) return;
    var isHoriz=(upTo%2===1);
    ctx.save();
    ctx.setLineDash([5,4]);
    ctx.lineWidth=0.8;
    ctx.strokeStyle='rgba(80,80,80,0.35)';
    ctx.beginPath();
    if(isHoriz){
      var ptL=px(xl[0],chain[upTo][1]);
      var ptR=px(xl[1],chain[upTo][1]);
      ctx.moveTo(ptL[0],ptL[1]); ctx.lineTo(ptR[0],ptR[1]);
    } else {
      var ptT=px(chain[upTo][0],yl[1]);
      var ptB=px(chain[upTo][0],yl[0]);
      ctx.moveTo(ptT[0],ptT[1]); ctx.lineTo(ptB[0],ptB[1]);
    }
    ctx.stroke();
    ctx.restore();
  }

  function annotate(upTo,rho,sig2){
    if(upTo===0){
      ann.style.borderColor='#1aab6d';
      ann.style.background='rgba(26,171,109,0.07)';
      ann.innerHTML='<b>Start:</b> chain begins far from the distribution. Watch it walk in.';
      return;
    }
    var isHoriz=(upTo%2===1);
    var step=Math.floor(upTo/2)+1;
    var curr=chain[upTo];
    var p=getParams();
    if(isHoriz){
      ann.style.borderColor='#2a72c8';
      ann.style.background='rgba(42,114,200,0.07)';
      ann.innerHTML='<b>Half-step '+step+'a &mdash; sample \u03b8\u2081 | \u03b8\u2082 = '+curr[1].toFixed(2)+':</b>'
        +' \u03b8\u2082 is <i>fixed</i> (dashed line). Draw \u03b8\u2081 from '
        +'N(\u03c1&middot;'+curr[1].toFixed(2)+', \u03c3\u00b2(1&minus;\u03c1\u00b2))'
        +' = N('+(p.rho*curr[1]).toFixed(2)+', '+(p.sig2*(1-p.rho*p.rho)).toFixed(2)+')'
        +' &rarr; \u03b8\u2081 = '+curr[0].toFixed(2)+'. Move <b>horizontally</b>.';
    } else {
      ann.style.borderColor='#e8793a';
      ann.style.background='rgba(232,121,58,0.07)';
      ann.innerHTML='<b>Half-step '+step+'b &mdash; sample \u03b8\u2082 | \u03b8\u2081 = '+curr[0].toFixed(2)+':</b>'
        +' \u03b8\u2081 is <i>fixed</i> (dashed line). Draw \u03b8\u2082 from '
        +'N(\u03c1&middot;'+curr[0].toFixed(2)+', \u03c3\u00b2(1&minus;\u03c1\u00b2))'
        +' = N('+(p.rho*curr[0]).toFixed(2)+', '+(p.sig2*(1-p.rho*p.rho)).toFixed(2)+')'
        +' &rarr; \u03b8\u2082 = '+curr[1].toFixed(2)+'. Move <b>vertically</b>.';
    }
  }

  function draw(upTo,rho,sig2){
    ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
    drawContours(rho,sig2);
    drawAxes();
    for(var i=1;i<=upTo&&i<chain.length;i++){
      var age=upTo-i;
      var alpha=Math.max(0.15,1-age*0.04);
      var p1=px(chain[i-1][0],chain[i-1][1]);
      var p2=px(chain[i][0],chain[i][1]);
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(p1[0],p1[1]); ctx.lineTo(p2[0],p2[1]);
      ctx.lineWidth=i===upTo?2.5:1.5;
      var baseCol=i%2===1?'42,114,200':'232,121,58';
      ctx.strokeStyle='rgba('+baseCol+','+alpha+')';
      ctx.stroke();
    }
    drawGuide(upTo);
    var s=px(chain[0][0],chain[0][1]);
    ctx.beginPath();ctx.arc(s[0],s[1],7,0,2*Math.PI);
    ctx.fillStyle='#1aab6d';ctx.fill();
    if(upTo>0&&upTo<chain.length){
      var cp=px(chain[upTo][0],chain[upTo][1]);
      ctx.beginPath();ctx.arc(cp[0],cp[1],6,0,2*Math.PI);
      ctx.fillStyle='#8f7fd4';ctx.fill();
      ctx.strokeStyle='#333';ctx.lineWidth=1.2;ctx.stroke();
    }
    ctx.font='12px sans-serif'; ctx.textAlign='left';
    ctx.fillStyle='#1aab6d'; ctx.fillText('\u25cf start',                        pad+8,pad+18);
    ctx.fillStyle='#2a72c8'; ctx.fillText('\u2014 sample \u03b8\u2081|\u03b8\u2082', pad+8,pad+34);
    ctx.fillStyle='#e8793a'; ctx.fillText('\u2014 sample \u03b8\u2082|\u03b8\u2081', pad+8,pad+50);
    ctx.fillStyle='#8f7fd4'; ctx.fillText('\u25cf current',                       pad+8,pad+66);
    root.querySelector('#gb-lbl').textContent='Step: '+Math.floor(upTo/2)+' / '+N;
    annotate(upTo,rho,sig2);
  }

  function rebuild(){
    clearInterval(timer); playing=false;
    root.querySelector('#gb-play').textContent='\u25b6 Play';
    var p=getParams();
    chain=buildChain(p.rho,p.sig2);
    cur=0; draw(0,p.rho,p.sig2);
  }

  function redraw(){ var p=getParams(); draw(cur,p.rho,p.sig2); }

  rebuild();

  root.querySelector('#gb-step').addEventListener('click',function(){
    if(cur<chain.length-1){cur++;redraw();}
  });

  root.querySelector('#gb-reset').addEventListener('click',rebuild);

  root.querySelector('#gb-play').addEventListener('click',function(){
    var btn=this;
    if(playing){
      clearInterval(timer);playing=false;btn.textContent='\u25b6 Play';
    } else {
      playing=true; btn.textContent='\u23f8 Pause';
      var spd=parseInt(root.querySelector('#gb-spd').value);
      timer=setInterval(function(){
        if(cur<chain.length-1){cur++;redraw();}
        else{clearInterval(timer);playing=false;btn.textContent='\u25b6 Play';}
      },spd);
    }
  });

  root.querySelector('#gb-spd').addEventListener('input',function(){
    root.querySelector('#gb-spdv').textContent=this.value+'ms';
    if(playing){
      clearInterval(timer);
      var spd=parseInt(this.value),btn=root.querySelector('#gb-play');
      timer=setInterval(function(){
        if(cur<chain.length-1){cur++;redraw();}
        else{clearInterval(timer);playing=false;btn.textContent='\u25b6 Play';}
      },spd);
    }
  });

  root.querySelector('#gb-rho').addEventListener('input',function(){
    root.querySelector('#gb-rhov').textContent=parseFloat(this.value).toFixed(2);
    rebuild();
  });

  root.querySelector('#gb-var').addEventListener('input',function(){
    root.querySelector('#gb-varv').textContent=parseFloat(this.value).toFixed(1);
    rebuild();
  });

},300);
</script>
```

## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler: HW5 Problem 3]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 57%;"}

Consider the model

$$
X_i \mid \mu,\lambda \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
N\left(\mu,\frac{1}{\lambda}\right),
\qquad
\mu\sim N(m_0,v_0),
\qquad
\lambda\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(a_0,b_0),
$$

where $\mu\perp\lambda$ a priori.

:::

. . .


[Let's derive the full conditionals.]{style="color: red; font-size: 2em; display: block; text-align: center; margin-top: 1rem;"}




## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler: HW5 Problem 3, cont'd]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}

The full conditional distributions are:

- $$\mu\mid\lambda,\mathbf{x} \sim N(m_n,v_n), \quad \text{where } m_n=\frac{n\lambda\bar{x}+m_0/v_0}{n\lambda+1/v_0}, \quad v_n=\left(n\lambda+\frac{1}{v_0}\right)^{-1}$$

- $$\lambda\mid\mu,\mathbf{x} \sim \operatorname{Gamma}\left(a_0+\frac{n}{2},\; b_0+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\right)$$


Let's set up our parameters first:
$m_0=5, v_0=0.5, a_0=1, b_0=4$

```{r, echo=TRUE}
library(coda)

# Parameters
m0 <- 5
v0 <- 0.5
a0 <- 1
b0 <- 4

# Data
x <- scan(url("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jkstatai/Rice_Fa26_STAT_425/main/docs/Data/school1.dat"))
n <- length(x)
xbar <- mean(x)
```

:::


## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler: HW5 Problem 3, cont'd]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 65%;"}

``` {.r code-line-numbers="1-29|1-4|6-8|10-15|17-21|10-21|1-29"}
# Storage
n_iter <- 10000
mu <- numeric(n_iter)
lambda <- numeric(n_iter)

# Initial values
mu[1] <- xbar
lambda[1] <- 1 / var(x)

# Gibbs sampling
for (t in 2:n_iter) {
  # 1. Sample mu | lambda, x
  vn <- 1 / (n * lambda[t-1] + 1/v0)
  mn <- vn * (n * lambda[t-1] * xbar + m0/v0)
  mu[t] <- rnorm(1, mn, sqrt(vn))
  
  # 2. Sample lambda | mu, x
  an <- a0 + n/2
  bn <- b0 + 0.5 * sum((x - mu[t])^2)
  lambda[t] <- rgamma(1, shape = an, rate = bn)
}

# Burn-in and analysis
burn_in <- 2000
mu_samp <- mu[(burn_in + 1):n_iter]
lambda_samp <- lambda[(burn_in + 1):n_iter]

mu_mcmc <- mcmc(mu_samp)
lambda_mcmc <- mcmc(lambda_samp)
```

```{r}
# Storage
n_iter <- 10000
mu <- numeric(n_iter)
lambda <- numeric(n_iter)

# Initial values
mu[1] <- xbar
lambda[1] <- 1 / var(x)

# Gibbs sampling
for (t in 2:n_iter) {
  # 1. Sample mu | lambda, x
  vn <- 1 / (n * lambda[t-1] + 1/v0)
  mn <- vn * (n * lambda[t-1] * xbar + m0/v0)
  mu[t] <- rnorm(1, mn, sqrt(vn))
  
  # 2. Sample lambda | mu, x
  an <- a0 + n/2
  bn <- b0 + 0.5 * sum((x - mu[t])^2)
  lambda[t] <- rgamma(1, shape = an, rate = bn)
}

# Burn-in and analysis
burn_in <- 2000
mu_samp <- mu[(burn_in + 1):n_iter]
lambda_samp <- lambda[(burn_in + 1):n_iter]

mu_mcmc <- mcmc(mu_samp)
lambda_mcmc <- mcmc(lambda_samp)
```

## [MCMC - Diagnostics: did the chain converge?]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 68%;"}

After running Gibbs, we need to check the chain actually worked. Three key tools:

. . .

**Trace plot** — plot $\mu^{(t)}$ and $\lambda^{(t)}$ over iterations. 
A good chain looks like a "hairy caterpillar" — mixing freely, not drifting or getting stuck.

. . .

**ACF (Autocorrelation Function)** — measures how correlated consecutive draws are.
Good mixing = ACF drops to zero quickly after lag 0.

. . .

**Effective Sample Size (ESS)** — because MCMC draws are *dependent*, 8000 draws $\neq$ 8000 independent samples. ESS tells you the equivalent number of independent draws.

$$\text{ESS} = \frac{M}{1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^\infty \text{ACF}(k)}$$

. . .

> For $\mu$: ESS ≈ 4885. For $\lambda$: ESS ≈ 4811. Both are high — the chain mixed well.

:::



## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler: HW5 Problem 3, cont'd]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}

```{r, echo=TRUE}
effectiveSize(mcmc(mu_samp))
effectiveSize(mcmc(lambda_samp))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(mu_samp, main = "ACF of mu")
acf(lambda_samp, main = "ACF of lambda")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

:::


## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler: HW5 Problem 3, cont'd]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}

```{r, echo=TRUE}
plot(mu_mcmc, main = "Trace & Density of mu")
```

:::

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}


## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler: HW5 Problem 3, cont'd]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}

Evaluate the marginal posterior density $p(\lambda \mid \mathbf{x})$ analytically up to a normalizing constant and overlay this density on your plot.

```{r, fig.height=5}
S <- sum((x - xbar)^2)
post_lambda <- function(lam) {
  lam <- ifelse(lam <= 0, NA, lam)
  part1 <- lam^(a0 + n/2 - 1) * (n * v0 + 1/lam)^(-0.5)
  part2 <- exp(-lam * (S + (n * v0 / (v0 + 1/(n*lam))) * (xbar - m0)^2) / 2 - b0 * lam)
  part1 * part2
}

norm_const <- integrate(post_lambda, lower = 0.001, upper = Inf)$value
grid <- seq(0.001, 0.15, length = 500)
dens <- sapply(grid, post_lambda) / norm_const

plot(density(lambda_samp),
     main = "Posterior of lambda | x",
     xlab = "lambda",
     xlim = c(0, 0.15),
     ylim = c(0, max(dens) * 1.1),
     lwd = 2, col = "black")

lines(grid, dens, col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright",
       legend = c("Gibbs MCMC", "Analytical posterior"),
       col = c("black", "red"),
       lwd = 2)
```

:::


## [MCMC - Gibbs sampler & MH(package(coda))]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 65%;"}

-  You can technically wrap any numeric vector or matrix(`object` here) in `mcmc_obj <- mcmc(object)` , even if it isn't a "real" MCMC sequence. However - and this is key - doing so doesn't make it an MCMC chain in a statistical sense. It just labels it as one so that functions like `plot()`, `acf()`, and `effectiveSize()` can run without error.

| Function | Purpose |
|:----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| `effectiveSize(mcmc_obj)` | Computes **Effective Sample Size (ESS)** — measures chain independence. |
| `gelman.diag(mcmc.list_obj)` | **Gelman–Rubin diagnostic** for checking convergence across multiple chains. |
| `geweke.diag(mcmc_obj)` | **Geweke diagnostic** for within-chain convergence (compares early vs. late samples). |
| `heidel.diag(mcmc_obj)` | **Heidelberger–Welch test** for stationarity and convergence. |
| `raftery.diag(mcmc_obj)` | **Raftery–Lewis diagnostic** estimating chain length needed for precision. |

:::

## MCMC - Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
Let's recap of Key Concepts

-   **Step 1:** Propose a candidate sample from the proposal
    (transition) distribution\
    $$
    g(x_{t+1} \mid x_t)
    $$ For example, if the proposal is Normal,\
    $$
    g(x_{t+1} \mid x_t) = \mathcal{N}(x_t, \sigma^2)
    $$

-   **Step 2:** Accept the proposed value with probability\
    $$
    A(x_t \rightarrow x_{t+1})
    $$

Detail Balance Condition to reach stationary:
$\quad p(a) T(a \rightarrow b)=p(b) T(b \rightarrow a), \quad \forall a, b$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{f(a)}{NC} g(b \mid a) A(a \rightarrow b)=\frac{f(b)}{NC } g(a \mid b) A(b \rightarrow a)
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

## MCMC - Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm

::::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{f(a)}{NC} g(b \mid a) A(a \rightarrow b)=\frac{f(b)}{NC } g(a \mid b) A(b \rightarrow a)
\end{aligned}
$$ Rewrite the balance condition:

$$\frac{A(a \rightarrow b)}{A(b \rightarrow a)}=\underbrace{\frac{f(b)}{f(a)}}_{r_f} \times \underbrace{\frac{g(a \mid b)}{g(b \mid a)}}_{r_g}$$

-   **Scenario 1**:
    $r_f r_g<1, A(a \rightarrow b)=r_f r_g, A(b \rightarrow a)=1$

-   **Scenario 1**:
    $r_f r_g>1, A(a \rightarrow b)= 1, A(b \rightarrow a)=\frac{1}{r_f r_g}$

::: {.fragment .highlight-red}
So $A(a \rightarrow b)=\operatorname{min}\left(r_f r_g, 1\right)$
:::

This matches the expression shown in Dr. Marina Vannucci’s slides:

::: {.fragment .highlight-red}
$$
A(\theta_{t-1} \rightarrow \theta^* = \theta_t) = \rho\left(\theta^{(t-1)}, \theta^*\right)=\min \left\{\frac{p\left(\theta^* \mid x\right)}{p\left(\theta^{(t-1)} \mid x\right)} \frac{q\left(\theta^{(t-1)} \mid \theta^*\right)}{q\left(\theta^* \mid \theta^{(t-1)}\right)}, 1\right\}
$$
:::

$$
\theta^{(t)}=\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\theta^* \quad \text { with probability } \rho\left(\theta^{(t-1)}, \theta^*\right) \\
\theta^{(t-1)} \quad \text { with probability } \quad 1-\rho\left(\theta^{(t-1)}, \theta^*\right)
\end{array}\right.
$$
:::::

## [MCMC - Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm - Intuition]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
Let's assume the distribution is symmetric

$$
\frac{A(a \rightarrow b)}{A(b \rightarrow a)}=\underbrace{\frac{f(b)}{f(a)}}_{r_f} \times \underbrace{\frac{g(a \mid b)}{g(b \mid a)}}_{r_g} = \underbrace{\frac{f(b)}{f(a)}}_{r_f} = \frac{p(b)}{p(a)} = \frac{p\left(\theta^* \mid y\right)}{p\left(\theta^{(t-1)} \mid y\right)} = r
$$

$A(a \rightarrow b)=\operatorname{min}\left(1, \frac{f(b)}{f(a)}\right) =\operatorname{min}\left(1, \frac{p(b)}{p(a)}\right) = \operatorname{min}\left(1, \frac{p\left(\theta^* \mid y\right)}{p\left(\theta^{(t-1)} \mid y\right)}=r\right)$

-   If $r>1$:

    -   Intuition: Since $\theta^{(t-1)}$ is already in our set, we
        should include $\theta^*$ as it has a higher probability than
        $\theta^{(t-1)}$.
    -   Procedure: Accept $\theta^*$ into our set, i.e. set
        $\theta^{(s)}=\theta^*$.

-   If $r<1$ :

    -   Intuition: The relative frequency of $\theta$-values in our set
        equal to $\theta^*$ compared to those equal to $\theta^{(t-1)}$
        should be
        $p\left(\theta^* \mid y\right) / p\left(\theta^{(t-1)} \mid y\right)=r$.
        This means that for every instance of $\theta^{(t-1)}$, we
        should have only a "fraction" of an instance of a $\theta^*$
        value.
    -   Procedure: Set $\theta^{(t)}$ equal to either $\theta^*$ or
        $\theta^{(t-1)}$, with probability $r$ and $1-r$ respectively.
:::

## [MCMC - Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 57%;"}
Consider the file `school1.` dat which contains data on the amount of times students at a high school spent on studying or homework during an exam period. Suppose we fit the following model:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_i & \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mu, \sigma^2\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n \\
\mu & \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_0, \tau_0^2\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\mu_0=5, \tau_0^2=0.5$. Let us fix $\sigma^2=1$. Implement a Metropolis-Hastings:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
library(coda)

# Read data
y <- scan(url("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jkstatai/Rice_Fa26_STAT_425/main/docs/Data/school1.dat"))
n <- length(y)

# Known hyperparameters
mu0 <- 5
tau0_sq <- 0.5
sigma_sq <- 1

# Log-posterior: log p(mu | y) ∝ log p(y | mu) + log p(mu)
log_post <- function(mu, y, mu0, tau0_sq, sigma_sq) {
  log_lik <- sum(dnorm(y, mean = mu, sd = sqrt(sigma_sq), log = TRUE))
  log_prior <- dnorm(mu, mean = mu0, sd = sqrt(tau0_sq), log = TRUE)
  log_lik + log_prior
}
```
:::

## [MCMC - Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm, cont'd]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}

-   A proposal function for $\mu$ centered at the previously sampled value.

-  My proposal $\mu^* \sim q\left(\mu^* \mid \mu^{(0)}\right)=N\left(\mu^{(0)}, \sigma_p^2\right)$, where we can set $\mu^{(0)} = \bar{y}$

```{r, echo=TRUE}
mean(y)
```


-  $\mu^*=\mu^{(t-1)}+\varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim N\left(0, \sigma_p^2\right)$ Hence, $q\left(\mu^* \mid \mu^{(t-1)}\right)=N\left(\mu^{(t-1)}, \sigma_p^2\right)$

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Metropolis–Hastings sampler (Random-Walk proposal)
mh_sampler <- function(sigma_p, n_iter = 5000, burn_in = 1000) {
  mu <- numeric(n_iter)
  mu[1] <- mean(y)
  
  for (t in 2:n_iter) {
    mu_prop <- rnorm(1, mean = mu[t - 1], sd = sigma_p)
    log_r <- log_post(mu_prop, y, mu0, tau0_sq, sigma_sq) -
             log_post(mu[t - 1], y, mu0, tau0_sq, sigma_sq)
    if (log(runif(1)) < log_r) {
      mu[t] <- mu_prop
    } else {
      mu[t] <- mu[t - 1]
    }
  }
  
  # Drop burn-in and return MCMC object
  chain <- mcmc(mu[(burn_in + 1):n_iter])
  return(chain)
}
```
:::

## [MCMC - Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm, cont'd]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Run chain with sigma_p = 0.5
set.seed(425)
chain_small <- mh_sampler(sigma_p = 0.5)

# Summaries and plots
summary(chain_small)
```
:::

## [MCMC - Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm, contd)]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}

```{r, echo=TRUE}
traceplot(chain_small, main = "Trace Plot (sigma_p = 0.5)")
```
:::

## [MCMC - Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm, contd)]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
```{r, echo=TRUE}
densplot(chain_small, main = "Posterior Density (sigma_p = 0.5)")
```
:::

## [MCMC - Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm, cont'd]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
```{r, echo=TRUE}
autocorr.plot(chain_small, main = "Autocorrelation (sigma_p = 0.5)")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}

\(c\) After removing an appropriate burn-in, evaluate the acceptance rate and the autocorrelation for varying lags. Which value of $\sigma_p$ provides a better choice for the proposal function?

```{r, echo = TRUE}
# Acceptance rate function
acceptance_rate <- function(chain) {
  draws <- as.numeric(chain)
  mean(diff(draws) != 0)
}
acceptance_rate(chain_small)
```

[(This is just an arbitrary number I came up with — you should check your own chain.)]{style="color:red;"}

The pattern is likely to be:

-   $\sigma_p=2$ accepts $\sim 27 \%$ proposals $\rightarrow$ better exploration.

# JAGS - Just Another Gibbs Sampler

## [The Posterior That Looks Easy but Isn’t — JAGS Is Your Best Friend!]{.r-fit-text}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
Model:

$$
y_i \sim \text{Cauchy}(\theta, \sigma), \quad
\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10^2), \quad
\sigma \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 10)
$$

Posterior:

$$
p(\theta, \sigma \mid y)
\propto
\left[ \prod_{i=1}^n
\frac{1}{\pi \sigma \left(1 + \frac{(y_i - \theta)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)} \right]
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\theta^2}{2 \times 10^2}\right)
$$

It only has **two parameters**, yet the posterior is:

-   ❌ No full conditional — not a known distribution\
-   ❌ Non-conjugate — prior and likelihood don’t simplify\
-   ❌ No closed-form normalization — integral can’t be solved

Result: $p(\theta,\sigma|y)$ has **no analytic form**, no direct
sampler, and no closed expression.

> 🤢 Manual derivation stops here.
:::

## What Are BUGS and JAGS?

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
-   **BUGS (Bayesian inference Using Gibbs Sampling):**\
    Early Bayesian software (1990s, Cambridge) using Gibbs sampling.
    Versions include *Classic BUGS(1990s)*, *WinBUGS(Windows-only)*, and
    *OpenBUGS(open-source successor)*.

-   **JAGS (Just Another Gibbs Sampler):**\
    Developed by Martyn Plummer in 2003 as a **cross-platform**,
    **open-source**, and **R-integrated** version of BUGS.

> 💡 JAGS keeps the same model syntax as BUGS but adds flexibility,
> automatic Metropolis–within–Gibbs sampling, and modern extensibility.

![](martin_plummer.jpg){.absolute top="420" left="30" width="300"
height="250"}

![](bugs.jpg){.absolute top="350" left="570" width="420" height="350"}
:::

## Why JAGS

::::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
::: {.fragment .fade-in}
1.  **Doing MCMC by hand means:**
    -   Writing out **priors** and **likelihood**
    -   Deriving **full conditional posteriors** for Gibbs sampling\
    -   Specifying a **proposal distribution** for Metropolis–Hastings\
    -   Tracking the **update order** for every parameter
2.  As models grow complex, this becomes
    -   🔁 *tedious*,\
    -   🧮 *algebraically messy*, and\
    -   🚫 *often intractable.*
3.  You want to spend time **analyzing**, not deriving.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
> JAGS can help you solve this once you specify the prior and the
> likelihood!
:::
:::::

## Enter JAGS

-   **JAGS** automates MCMC sampling.\
-   You define your model using **BUGS-like syntax**.\
-   It automatically:
    -   Constructs the **posterior**\
    -   Performs **Gibbs / Metropolis-Hastings sampling**\
    -   Returns results to **R** through `rjags` or `R2jags`.

## How JAGS Samples Behind the Scenes

:::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
Even within Gibbs sampling, not all parameters have closed-form
conditionals.

JAGS handles this **automatically**:

| Parameter Type | Sampling Strategy | Description |
|------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------|
| Conjugate blocks | **Pure Gibbs** | Exact draws from known conditionals |
| Non-conjugate blocks | **Metropolis–within–Gibbs** | Uses adaptive random-walk MH inside Gibbs |
| Difficult continuous nodes | **Slice sampling** | Efficient for highly nonlinear posteriors |

So Gibbs and Metropolis **run in parallel**:

-   Each iteration updates some parameters by **Gibbs**, others by
    **Metropolis**\
-   JAGS adapts proposal scales automatically during burn-in\
-   You don’t need to code or tune anything

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
> 💡 *You define the model; JAGS decides the best sampler for each
> part.*
:::
::::

## BUGS syntax - Example 1

::: {style="font-size: 55%;"}
$y_i \sim N\left(\mu, \sigma^2\right),\quad \mu \sim N(0,100), \quad \sigma \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,10)$

``` {.BUGS code-line-numbers="1-4,5,9,13,15,16|5-6|9-11|13-14|1-16"}
# BUGS syntax (general form)
  "
  model {
    for (i in 1:N) {
      # Likelihood
      y[i] ~ distribution(parameter1, parameter2)   # stochastic: likelihood for data
    }
    
    # Priors for parameters
    parameter1 ~ prior_distribution1(hyperparameter_set1)   # prior for parameter1
    parameter2_raw ~ prior_distribution2(hyperparameter_set2)  # prior for parameter2 (before transformation)
    
    # Deterministic relationship (if needed)
    parameter2 <- g(parameter2_raw)    # e.g., transformation such as 1 / variance
  }
  "
```

Then, append the `model{}` block into the R code

``` {.r code-line-numbers="1,2,15,16|1-16"}
# Model specification
model_code <- 
  "
  model {
    for (i in 1:N) {
      y[i] ~ dnorm(mu, tau)  # likelihood for data
    }
    # Priors for parameters
    mu ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)      # Prior: mu ~ N(0, 100), in JAGS, always use precision = 1/100 = 0.01
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 10)     # Prior: sigma ~ Uniform(0, 10)
    tau <- pow(sigma, -2)    # Precision tau = 1 / sigma^2
  }
"

# Write model to file
writeLines(model_code, "model.txt")
```
:::

## BUGS syntax - Example 2

::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
$y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i+\varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \sim N\left(0, \sigma^2\right), \quad \beta_0 \sim N(0,1000), \beta_1 \sim N(0,1000), \sigma^2 \sim \operatorname{Inv-Gamma}(0.001,0.001)$

``` {.BUGS code-line-numbers="1-5,10,14,17,18|5-7|10-12|14-16|1-18"}
# BUGS syntax (general linear regression form)
  "
  model {
    for (i in 1:N) {
      # Likelihood
      y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau)             # stochastic: likelihood for data
      mu[i] <- beta0 + beta1 * x[i]        # deterministic: mean structure
    }

    # Priors for regression coefficients
    beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)                # Prior: β₀ ~ N(0, 1000)
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)                # Prior: β₁ ~ N(0, 1000)

    # Prior for error variance
    tau <- 1 / pow(sigma, 2)               # Precision = 1 / σ²
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)                  # Equivalent to Inv-Gamma(0.001, 0.001)
  }
  "
```

Then, append the `model{}` block into the R code

``` {.r code-line-numbers="1-2,16,17|1-17"}
# Model specification
model_code_2 <- 
  "
  model {
    for (i in 1:N) {
      y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau)             # likelihood for data
      mu[i] <- beta0 + beta1 * x[i]        # mean structure
    }
    beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)                # prior for intercept
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)                # prior for slope
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)                  # prior for standard deviation
    tau <- pow(sigma, -2)                  # precision = 1 / sigma^2
  }
  "

# Write model to file
writeLines(model_code_2, "model_2.txt")
```
:::

# [🚀 Hands-On with rjags: Let’s Build a Bayesian Model]{.r-fit-text}

## Example 1 (Cont'd)

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
Suppose we would like to run a model to draw inference about the mean
for the following model:

$$
y_i \sim N\left(\mu, \sigma^2\right)
$$

where $y_i$ are the data include 30 observations.

Priors are:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mu \sim N(0,100) \\
\sigma \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,10)
\end{gathered}
$$

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Ground Truth
rm(list=ls())
n = 30
mu = 1.12
sigma = 0.38

# Generate values (stochastic part of the model)
# In reality, you only observe 30 data points, and the true population mean 
# and variance are unknown. Our goal is to estimate these parameters.
set.seed(425)
y = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
```
:::

## Example 1 (Cont'd)

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
```{r, echo=TRUE}
df = data.frame(y)
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(df, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Simulated y", x = "y", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::

## Example 1 (Cont'd)

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
If we put `n = 10000`, it is indeed the bell shape!

```{r}
y_demo <- rnorm(10000, 1.12, 0.38)
df_demo <- data.frame(y_demo)
ggplot(df_demo, aes(x = y_demo)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..))+
  stat_function(fun = dnorm,
                  args = list(mean = 1.12, sd = 0.38),
                  color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Simulation with n = 10000", x = "x", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

```
:::

## Example 1 (Cont'd)

:::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
-   Recall our BUGS syntax: `writeLines(model_code, "model.txt")`

::: {.fragment .highlight-red}
-   You don't really need to specify `inits`
:::

```{r,echo=FALSE}
# Model specification
model_code <-
  "
  model {
    for (i in 1:N) {
      y[i] ~ dnorm(mu, tau)  # Likelihood
    }
    mu ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)      # Prior: mu ~ N(0, 100), in JAGS, always use precision
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 10)     # Prior: sigma ~ Uniform(0, 10)
    tau <- pow(sigma, -2)    # Precision tau = 1 / sigma^2
  }
  "

# Write model to file
writeLines(model_code, "model.txt")
```

``` {.r code-line-numbers="1-17|7-9,17||1-17"}
# Prepare data for JAGS
jagsData <- list(
  y = y,
  N = length(y)
)

# Initial values for the model
jags_inits <- function() {
  list(mu = rnorm(1, 0, 10), sigma = runif(1, 0, 10)) # priors
}

# Parameters to monitor
jags_params <- c("mu", "sigma","tau")

# Load rjags and run the model
library(rjags)
model_1 <- jags.model(file = "model.txt", data = jagsData, inits = jags_inits, n.chains = 3)
```

```{r}
# Prepare data for JAGS
jagsData <- list(
  y = y,
  N = length(y)
)

# Initial values for the model
jags_inits <- function() {
  list(mu = rnorm(1, 0, 10), sigma = runif(1, 0, 10)) # priors
}

# Parameters to monitor
jags_params <- c("mu", "sigma","tau")

# Load rjags and run the model
library(rjags)
model_1 <- jags.model(file = "model.txt", data = jagsData, inits = jags_inits, n.chains = 3)
```
::::

## Example 1 (Cont'd)

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Sample from posterior
samples <- coda.samples(model_1, variable.names = jags_params, n.iter = 2000, n.burnin = 1000)

# Convert to matrix for easier manipulation
output <- as.matrix(samples)

# Extract results
mu_samples <- output[, "mu"]
sigma_samples <- output[, "sigma"]
tau_samples <- output[,"tau"]

# Summary statistics
# posterior prediction
mean(mu_samples)
mean(sigma_samples)
mean(tau_samples)
```

-   Recall our ground truth: `mu = 1.12`, `sigma = 0.38`. What will you
    conclude about the result from JAGS.

## Example 2 (Cont'd)

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
Simple Linear Regression: We have the data of 48 pigs with body weight
measured at 9 successive weeks. Suppose we would like to fit the model:
for $i=1, \cdots, 432$

$$
y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i+\epsilon_i \quad \epsilon_i \sim N\left(0, \sigma^2\right)
$$

Priors are:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\beta_0 \sim N(0,1000) \\
\beta_1 \sim N(0,1000) \\
\sigma^2 \sim \text { Inv- } \operatorname{Gamma}(0.001,0.001)
\end{gathered}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
rm(list=ls())
# Ground Truth
set.seed(425)
N <- 48
beta0_true <- 2
beta1_true <- 0.5
sigma_true <- 1
# Generate synthetic data
x <- rnorm(N, 5, 2)
y <- rnorm(N, beta0_true + beta1_true * x, sigma_true)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE}
# Model specification
model_code_2 <- 
  "
  model {
    for (i in 1:N) {
      y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau2)             # likelihood for data
      mu[i] <- beta0 + beta1 * x[i]        # mean structure
    }
    beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)                # prior for intercept
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)                # prior for slope
    sigma2 ~ dunif(0, 100)                  # prior for standard deviation
    tau2 <- pow(sigma2, -2)                  # precision = 1 / sigma^2
  }
  "

# Write model to file
writeLines(model_code_2, "model_2.txt")
```
:::

## Example 2 (Cont'd)

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
Recall our BUGS syntax: `writeLines(model_code_2, "model_2.txt")`

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Prepare data for JAGS
jags_data <- list(
  N = N,
  x = x,
  y = y
)

# Initial values for chains
inits <- function() {
  list(beta0 = rnorm(1, 0, 1),
       beta1 = rnorm(1, 0, 1),
       sigma2 = runif(1, 0, 5))
}

# Parameters to monitor
params <- c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma2", "tau2")

# Load rjags and run the model
library(rjags)
model_2 <- jags.model("model_2.txt",
                    data = jags_data,
                    inits = inits,
                    n.chains = 3)
```
:::

## Example 2 (Cont'd)

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
```{r, echo=TRUE}
samples_2 <- coda.samples(model_2, variable.names = params, n.iter = 3000, n.burnin = 1000)

# Convert to matrix for easier manipulation
output_2 <- as.matrix(samples_2)

# Extract results
beta0_samples <- output_2[, "beta0"]
beta1_samples <- output_2[, "beta1"]
sigma_samples_2 <- output_2[,"sigma2"]
tau_samples_2 <- output_2[,"tau2"]

# Summary statistics
# posterior prediction
mean(beta0_samples)
mean(beta1_samples)
mean(sigma_samples_2)
mean(tau_samples_2)
```

-   Recall our ground truth: `beta0_true = 2`, `beta1_true = 0.5`,
    `sigma_true=1`. What will you conclude about the result from JAGS.
:::

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=6, echo=TRUE}

```

## [Example 3: Random-Intercept Model in Action (Optional practice)]{.r-fit-text}

:::: {style="font-size: 55%;"}
Same pig dataset, assume intercept is different for each pig Data
likelihood: for $i=1, \cdots, 48, j=1, \cdots, 9$

$y_{i j}=\beta_0+\theta_i+\beta_1 x_{i j}+\varepsilon_{i j}, \quad \theta_i \sim N\left(0, \tau^2\right), \quad \varepsilon_{i j} \sim N\left(0, \sigma^2\right)$

$\beta_0 \sim N(0,1000), \quad \beta_1 \sim N(0,1000)$

$\tau^2 \sim \operatorname{Inv-Gamma}(0.001,0.001), \quad \sigma^2 \sim \operatorname{Inv-Gamma}(0.001,0.001)$

``` bugs
# Model specification
model_code <- 
  "
  model {
    for (i in 1:N_pig) {
      for (j in 1:N_obs) {
        y[i, j] ~ dnorm(mu[i, j], tau_eps)
        mu[i, j] <- beta0 + theta[i] + beta1 * x[i, j]
      }
      theta[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau_theta)
    }
    beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
    tau_eps <- pow(sigma, -2)
    sigma_theta ~ dunif(0, 100)
    tau_theta <- pow(sigma_theta, -2)
  }
  "

# Write model to file
writeLines(model_code, "model.txt")
```
